paras: The lynching of Isaac and Puss Kirkpatrick was the killing of a Black ("colored") married couple by a mob near Gallatin, Tennessee, about midnight on April 18, 1888, in which the wife was hanged and the husband shot. Puss Kirkpatrick had been suspected of burning a nearby country house, while her husband, who was not suspected, was believed to have been killed because he recognized members of the mob. A wire dispatch carried the story across the country within a day, and several Northern and Western papers printed it under headlines condemning mob law.

The Kirkpatricks lived in a cabin about five miles from Gallatin. Some time earlier, the country residence of John Kerley had burned to the ground with its entire contents, and suspicion had fallen on Puss Kirkpatrick. The Gallatin correspondent of the Nashville American stressed that "this was only suspicion" and that Isaac Kirkpatrick, her "aged husband," was not suspected of any part in the burning.

About midnight, a group described as "a mob" in some versions and "a band of men" in others took the couple from their cabin. The woman was hanged from a tree in her night clothes, and the man was shot through the brain.

Early the next morning Jim McCollough, walking along a country road, saw what he took to be a woman in a night-dress hiding behind a tree and nearly stumbled over Isaac Kirkpatrick's body lying beside the road. At the tree he found the woman hanging dead, her feet almost touching the ground, and he hurried to report it in town. Both bodies were then brought to Gallatin, where, according to the wire account, they were received by "hundreds of negroes."

A coroner and jury of inquest went to the spot and reported that the woman died of strangulation and the husband of a pistol-shot wound, inflicted "by parties unknown." Nearly every account repeated the theory that Isaac Kirkpatrick had recognized some of the party and was shot to keep him from exposing them. The dispatches said the deed was condemned on all sides by "law-abiding citizens," and a separate Gallatin dispatch of April 20 said such citizens "deprecate the lynching."

Beyond the inquest's finding of "parties unknown," no report of arrests, an indictment or a trial appears in the coverage. At the end of the year a list of "Victims of Judge Lynch" entered the case under April 18, describing the couple as "suspected of arson."

Most papers took the story from a special dispatch to the Nashville American, sent by wire under a Nashville dateline of April 19. On April 20 it ran in the Memphis Appeal as "A Colored Woman Lynched," in the Richmond Dispatch as "Suspected Incendiaries Lynched," and in the Fort Worth Daily Gazette, the Wichita Eagle and the Rock Island Argus.

Headline writers diverged sharply in tone. One paper headed the wire "Tennessee Fire Bugs Hurried to Eternity," treating the victims as arsonists. By contrast, the Wichita Eagle wrote of a couple "inhumanly murdered" and of "cowardly lynchers," and the Rock Island Argus called the affair "Disgraceful and Dastardly" and "the Culmination of the Diabolism of Mob Law." The Emporia Weekly News reprinted the dispatch on April 26 under the ironic heading "Southern Chivalry."

A fuller Gallatin account, with McCollough's discovery and the inquest, appeared in the Hillsboro, Ohio, News-Herald on April 26, which called the killing "one of the most sensational tragedies in the history of this county." Weekly news digests reduced the story to a line or two, saying that the couple were taken "on the 19th" and were suspected of arson, or that the woman was lynched "it is supposed for incendiarism."

The dispatches dated April 19 placed the killing "last night," about midnight, and the year-end list gave April 18. The Rock Island Argus, re-dating the wire to April 20, said "Thursday night" (April 19), and a weekly digest said "the 19th," but the Argus also had the bodies reaching Gallatin "Thursday evening," which fits a killing the night before.
The fuller accounts held that only Puss Kirkpatrick was suspected of the Kerley fire, while the shorter Richmond and Wyoming versions said both were suspected of incendiarism.

Both Kirkpatricks were killed by an unofficial 'mob', 'band of men' or 'lynching party' acting without authority, the wife as punishment for a suspected house-burning (A1, A2, A10); a coroner's jury attributed the deaths to 'parties unknown' (A10).
The Nashville American's wire story (A1), a separately worded Gallatin dispatch with the inquest (A10) and a third short Gallatin dispatch (A15) agree on the seizure, hanging and shooting.
